And I tracked the weather pretty closely because I was going to be subject to it. I remember 102, 103. I don't remember 110, 110, 110, 110. It's obvious to me and I think of course the experts have said this and so my opinion matters much less than theirs That the climate is changing and that it's making it much more difficult To enjoy some of the things that I think we all enjoy like being outdoors playing sports It's the point where when my kids are at school They're saying that they'll do some water activities in the morning my kids are little and four and two and And then keep them inside the rest of the day. That's not what I want for them. But you're right that the Inflation Reduction Act, which despite its name, was actually the biggest climate bill in modern American history. The estimates are that it's going to help us reduce our emissions by 30% by 2030. And that's dramatic. And it's already, I think we're just beginning to see its impact. In my district, there's a company called Canadian Solar that's building a solar panel manufacturing plant in Mesquite. And it's a $250 million investment. It's going to create 100, 1,500 jobs. And they're basing it basically on the subsidies from the Inflation Reduction Act. I was with the Norwegian ambassador a few weeks ago in my office and she was saying that the Europeans are actually upset because so much of their kind of green energy manufacturing is going to come to the United States now because they can't keep up with the subsidies and the benefits that we're offering for that. She mentioned that there was a Norwegian battery company. that was going to open a plant in Norway, but now it's going to do it in Georgia. So we're at the beginning of this. But for Texas, we're in energy state, and we're always going to be in energy state. And we're the number one, wind energy state in the country. We're number two in solar. We have nuclear power as part of our mix. And of course, oil and gas is always going to be important. And one of the things I do get frustrated with on our side is, I think it's an unrealistic conversation around the use of oil and gas, and whether or not we're going to be able to completely transition away from it. I don't see that happening. But what I do think we can do is meet it from a couple of different ends. We can reduce emissions by some of the incentives that we have in place to capture methane, to be better in our extraction processes, things like that, and also reduce in our own usage what we're putting out. Your house will be more efficient, your cars will be more efficient, that our buildings will be more efficient. We can come at it from those different ways, and we have to look into carbon recapture technology and trying to draw down some of the things that we've already put out. We're always going to be an energy state. And I think that's for Texans and for somebody who represents Texas and Congress and wants to represent us in the Senate, I'll always also make sure that I'm protecting our economy and that, to me, this is about growing our energy economy, not taking away jobs. And that's what this, I guess, if you want to use the word transition will be that we create more jobs in some of these fields, but I don't see it taking away. And it doesn't have to be taking away because our energy needs are actually just going to continue to grow.
